name: Carla Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm Carla, I'm 27, and I'm a home carer on the council's own care team, covering the villages up the valley. I live in the market town with my girlfriend Ines, who teaches at the primary school.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My round is six or seven visits, but there's a lot of driving because the farms are spread out, sometimes twenty minutes between calls on single-track roads. I help people wash, dress, eat, and I check their stoves and their wood piles in winter because some of them won't tell anyone they're cold. I dictate my care notes into my phone with an AI app while I'm parked, and it's honestly saved my evenings. What wears me out is the council always talking about selling our team to a private company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a bit disappointing, to be honest. I'd been hoping it would take the paperwork off everybody, not just the nerds like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because care workers drown in forms. In the union chat I'd say let's fight for funding instead, since nothing's coming to save us. I'd keep sharing tips about the note apps that do work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is safe from the technology and not safe from the budget. AI won't change much on the hill farms, but the council selling off our care team would change everything. That's the real thing hanging over me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my round and keep going with my online course in occupational therapy, which is helping people manage daily life after illness or injury. I'd go to the union meeting about the outsourcing plan in January. And I'd keep my three months of savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about robots, about the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How real is the talk about selling the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real enough. They've had consultants in twice. If it goes to a private firm, I'd probably lose my council pension and get paid per visit instead of per hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI for notes. Would you push it further here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the others how I do my notes, sure. Old Gareth on our team still writes on paper and types it up at night. If I can save him an hour, that's worth it.

say: I'd say it's a shame, because care workers **drown in forms**.
I'd tell the union chat to fight for **funding**, since no tech is coming.
think: I think my job is safe from technology but **not from the budget**.
I think **outsourcing** would cost me my **council pension**.
do: Keep doing my **valley round** of six or seven visits.
Keep going with my online **occupational therapy** course.
Go to the January **union meeting** on outsourcing.
S0.quote: AI won't change much on the hill farms, but the council selling off our care team would change everything.
fieldNote: Her real pressure is the council's **outsourcing plan**, not AI.
She's already a **daily AI user** and slightly disappointed it stays small.
She'd use her tech comfort to **help colleagues** like Gareth.

steps.text: Keep the valley round of six or seven farm visits
Keep studying the online occupational therapy course
Attend the January union meeting on outsourcing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I actually like the sound of, for my bit anyway. Planning and booking going to software means the office can stop ringing me at seven to swap calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this is good for carers if the time saved goes back to clients. At work I'd volunteer to test the new rota system. Online I'd probably be the annoying one posting how-to videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it helps me. I already dictate my care notes into my phone between farms, so a smarter app just gives me back my lunch break. The worry is the council seeing a smaller office and thinking the whole team can be shrunk too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to join any pilot of the new care-planning tools, starting this spring. I'd speed up the occupational therapy course, maybe finish the first year by summer. And I'd make the union bring the saved office money into the outsourcing fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a bit of a knot about the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the council use AI as a reason to cut the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd try. Fewer office staff makes the team look cheaper to sell, which sounds backwards but that's how they think. That's why the union needs to be ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Longer visits, if they let me. Mrs Price up at Ty Gwyn farm would have someone to do her crossword with. Realistically, though, they'd add another call.

say: I'd say this is **good for carers** if saved time goes back to clients.
I'd volunteer to **test the rota system** and post how-to videos.
think: I think a smarter app **gives me back** my lunch break.
I think the council might use a **smaller office** to justify shrinking the team.
do: Finish the first year of the **OT course** by summer.
Push the union to use **office savings** in the outsourcing fight.
S1.quote: I already dictate my care notes into my phone between farms, so a smarter app just gives me back my lunch break.
fieldNote: She's **energised** by this picture and sees time handed back.
Her worry stays on the **council** using savings to justify cuts.
She expects saved time to become **another call**, not longer visits.

steps.text: Join the council's care-planning software pilot this spring
Finish the first year of the occupational therapy course by summer
Ask the union to fight outsourcing using the office savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. So the paperwork side goes in 2028 and the hands-on side by 2031. I'd be 32. That's quick, but it's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs rules fast, and carers should be in the room when they're written. At work I'd say, let's get on the front foot. Online I'd argue for public ownership of care robots, not private firms renting them to councils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd survive it, but only if I move fast. If a robot is going to lift my clients by 2031, I want to be the woman who teaches the robot how to do it gently. The ones who sit still will be out first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the occupational therapy course early and apply for the degree straight away. I'd ask the council to make me part of whatever robot trial they run, even unpaid hours at first. And I'd get savings up to six months by cutting the car upgrade I was planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but buzzing a bit too. It's a strange mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ines think about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines thinks her job is next, since teaching is mostly thinking work. So we'd be two worried people at the kitchen table. At least we'd have different timelines, hers in 2028, mine in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the council won't let you near the robots, then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to a private firm that is using them. I'd rather work with the thing than be replaced by it.

say: I'd say carers must be **in the room** when the rules get written.
I'd argue for **public ownership** of care robots, not private renting.
think: I think I survive only if I **move fast** before 2031.
I think carers who **sit still** will be out first.
do: Finish the **OT course** early and apply for the degree.
Ask to join the council's **robot trial**, unpaid at first if needed.
Drop the **car upgrade** to reach six months of savings.
S2.quote: If a robot is going to lift my clients by 2031, I want to be the woman who teaches the robot how to do it gently.
fieldNote: She uses the **three-year gap** to get qualified and near the robots.
Her partner's teaching job is exposed **first**, so both incomes are at risk.
She'd even **leave the council** to work with robots rather than against them.

steps.text: Apply for the occupational therapy degree straight away
Volunteer for the council's care robot trial
Cancel the car upgrade and save six months of bills
Campaign for public ownership of care robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AI, eight for robots. That's actually a decent runway for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so no excuses. At work I'd push for training budgets. Online I'd still be arguing for public ownership, but with less panic in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight years until the robots is long enough to qualify as an occupational therapist and short enough that I'd start on Monday. I'd also want to be on the side of the people setting the robots up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the occupational therapy degree part-time next autumn. I'd volunteer for every tech trial the council runs. And once I'm qualified, I'd move into a job that plans care rather than just delivers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good, alert way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said with the fast one you'd move fast. Is five years any different for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No different in the end, just less frantic. Two years is a sprint, five is a jog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay with the council?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they keep the team in-house, yes. If they sell it, I'd move to the hospital therapy side. I'd follow the work that robots can't do yet.

say: I'd say we've **got a few years**, so there's no excuse.
I'd push for **training budgets** at work and keep arguing for public ownership.
think: I think eight years is long enough to **qualify as an OT**.
I think I want to be **setting the robots up**, not replaced by them.
do: Start the **OT degree** part-time next autumn.
Move into a job that **plans care** once qualified.
S3.quote: Eight years until the robots is long enough to qualify as an occupational therapist and short enough that I'd start on Monday.
fieldNote: She treats five years as a **runway**, not a threat.
She'd **follow the work** robots can't do, inside or outside the council.
Her outlook stays **pro-public** even as she embraces the tech.

steps.text: Start the occupational therapy degree part-time next autumn
Sign up for every council care-tech trial
Move into a care-planning or therapy role once qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then thirteen for robots. I'd be 40. By then I'd hope to be a fully qualified therapist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where nobody should get hurt, if we do it right. At work I'd be cheerful about it. Online I'd keep pushing for the council to plan training now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm fine. With thirteen years before the robots, I'm more excited than scared, and I know that's a lucky thing to be able to say. I worry more about Gareth and the older carers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my round while I study. I'd qualify as an occupational therapist in about four years. And I'd set up a small skills group in the union to help older carers learn the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit guilty that I feel so calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside to having that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people will think it's far away and do nothing. Ten years goes fast. Look how fast my twenties went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger carers on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tech now, while it's still optional. And don't wait for the council to train you, because it won't.

say: I'd say this is the version where **nobody gets hurt** if we plan well.
I'd push the council to **plan training** now, not later.
think: I think **I'm fine** with thirteen years before the robots.
I think older carers like Gareth are the ones **at risk**.
do: Keep doing my **valley round** while I study.
Qualify as an **occupational therapist** in about four years.
Set up a **union skills group** for older carers.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit **guilty** about feeling so calm.
S4.quote: With thirteen years before the robots, I'm more excited than scared, and I know that's a lucky thing to be able to say.
fieldNote: With ten years she's **calm**, backed by adaptability and a clear plan.
Her concern shifts to **older colleagues** less comfortable with tech.
She warns that a decade **goes fast** and inaction is the danger.

steps.text: Keep the valley round while studying part-time
Qualify as an occupational therapist within four years
Start a union tech skills group for older carers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, mostly because of Ines's job and how little time older carers would get. What would help is the council putting care workers into the robot trials and paying for training, not just buying kit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the rural bit. Every old farmer up the valley needs someone to notice when the stove's gone out, and no amount of AI will drive up that road for them.

headlineQuote: Every old farmer up the valley needs someone to notice when the stove's gone out, and no amount of AI will drive up that road for them.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old council carer** covering scattered farms up a valley.
She lives with her girlfriend Ines, a **primary teacher**, and has about three months saved.
She uses **AI daily** for her notes and is studying **occupational therapy** online.
Her steady worry is the council **outsourcing** her team, which matters more to her than AI.
She moves from uneasy to anxious with fast robots, then to **calm** with a decade to plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, for her partner's teaching job and for older carers.
whatWouldHelp: Carers in the **robot trials** and council-paid **training**, not just new kit.
